blocks.title: Keeping Information Safe
blocks.subtitle: Confidentiality, integrity and availability in practice

blocks.text:
Data is valuable to its owner and to anyone who would steal, alter or hold it to ransom. Data security is the set of practices that keeps information confidential, correct and available to the people entitled to it.

Technology is only part of the answer. Most incidents begin with a weak password, an unpatched system or a convincing email.

items.label: Goals of the CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
Independent proofs of identity in two-factor authentication
Deadline to report many personal-data breaches under the EU's GDPR

blocks.heading: Three goals
blocks.text: **Confidentiality** means only authorised people can read the data. **Integrity** means it cannot be changed without detection. **Availability** means it is there when needed. Every control, from a door lock to a backup, serves one or more of these goals, and a good design balances them against cost and convenience.

steps.text: **Classify.** Know what data you hold, where it is and how sensitive it is. You cannot protect what you have not identified.
**Control access.** Grant each person and system the least access needed, and verify identity with more than a password.
**Encrypt.** Protect data in storage and in transit so that a stolen disk or intercepted message reveals nothing.
**Monitor and back up.** Log activity, watch for anomalies and keep tested backups that an attacker cannot reach.

points.title: Detect
points.text: Logging, monitoring and alerting on suspicious activity.

points.title: Respond
points.text: Contain an incident, investigate it and notify those affected.

points.title: Recover
points.text: Restore systems and data, then learn from what happened.

blocks.heading: People and process
blocks.text: Attackers usually take the easiest route, and that is often a person. Phishing emails, reused passwords and misdirected files cause a large share of breaches. Regular training, multi-factor authentication, prompt patching and a rehearsed incident plan prevent more harm than most expensive tools.

items.title: Least privilege
items.text: Give every account only the access its task requires.

items.title: Multi-factor authentication
items.text: Combining something you know, have or are to prove identity.

items.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
items.text: Protecting stored data and data moving over networks.

items.title: 3-2-1 backups
items.text: Three copies, on two kinds of media, one of them off-site.

items.title: Zero trust
items.text: Verify every request, whatever network it comes from.

blocks.text: Security is not a product you install. It is a habit an organisation keeps.

blocks.heading: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Stronger controls cost time and convenience, and people work around controls that obstruct them. Cloud services move data outside the organisation's walls. Laws in different countries impose different duties. Good security therefore starts from risk: what could go wrong, how likely it is, and what it would cost.

blocks.question: A ransomware attack that encrypts a hospital's files mainly harms which goal?
blocks.explanation: The data are still there but cannot be used, so availability is lost. Tested offline backups are the main defence.

blocks.question: Which is an example of two-factor authentication?
options: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
blocks.explanation: The factors must be of different kinds: something you know and something you have.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Threat**: something that could cause harm. **Vulnerability**: a weakness a threat can use. **Risk**: likelihood combined with impact. **Phishing**: deceptive messages that trick people into revealing secrets. **Incident response**: the planned handling of a breach.
